title: “THE HEART IS DECEITFUL ABOVE ALL THINGS” — BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS ONLY PART OF THE MESSAGE
paragraphs: “THE HEART IS DECEITFUL ABOVE ALL THINGS” — BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS ONLY PART OF THE MESSAGE

You have probably heard this verse used to tell you never to trust your heart. But keep reading. The next words reveal who can search the heart no human being can fully understand—and a few verses later, Jeremiah cries out for the only healing deep enough to reach it.
There are Bible verses we quote so often that eventually we stop hearing them.
Words printed across coffee mugs, devotionals, T-shirts, and social media graphics.
And somewhere between memorizing the verse and repeating it, we can accidentally stop asking what God was actually saying.
Jeremiah 17:9 may be one of those verses.
“The heart is deceitful above all things…”
Maybe somebody quoted it to you after you made a terrible decision.
Maybe you followed your feelings into a relationship that wounded you.
Maybe you trusted someone you should not have trusted.
Maybe you convinced yourself that something sinful was harmless because it felt right at the time.
Maybe you looked straight at a warning sign and renamed it “peace.”
Maybe you prayed for God’s will while secretly begging Him to approve the decision you had already made.
And suddenly Jeremiah 17:9 sounded painfully personal.
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿāqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl, wəʾānuš hūʾ; mî yēḏāʿennū?
The heart is deceitful—crooked, insidious—above all, and desperately sick, grievously afflicted. Who can know it?
The Hebrew word translated “heart” is לֵב — lev.
In biblical Hebrew, the heart is more than the place where emotions happen. It is associated with the inner person—with thought, desire, intention, decision, understanding, and will.
And Jeremiah says something disturbing about it.
Then comes אָנֻשׁ — ʾānûš, a word carrying the sense of being desperately sick, grievously afflicted, even incurable in certain contexts.
And then Jeremiah asks the terrifying question:
That question should make us uncomfortable.
Because we spend enormous portions of our lives trusting the very thing Scripture warns can deceive us.
But is every feeling of relief the peace of God?
But when did happiness become the final test of holiness?
Your heart can lie to you.
Not merely that other people can deceive you.
Not merely that Satan can tempt you.
Not merely that culture can mislead you.
You can participate in deceiving yourself.
You can call cowardice “waiting on God.”
You can call disobedience “following your heart.”
You can call an idol “a blessing.”
You can even use spiritual vocabulary to protect something God has been asking you to surrender.
That is why this verse hurts.
Because Jeremiah does not merely expose the person sitting beside you.

He reaches past the Christian vocabulary, the worship playlist, the Bible highlighted in five colors, the church attendance, the Facebook Scripture posts, the ministry position, the theological arguments, the public testimony…
…and puts his finger on the place nobody else can see.
But here is where we have to be extremely careful.
But Jeremiah 17:9 is not the whole message.
Stop ending the sermon one verse too early.
Because the very next verse says:
אֲנִי יְהוָה חֹקֵר לֵב בֹּחֵן כְּלָיוֹת
ʾănî YHWH, ḥōqēr lēḇ, bōḥēn kəlāyōṯ…
You may not completely understand your own heart.
You may have buried something so deeply that you have constructed an entire personality around avoiding it.
You may have become so skilled at explaining your behavior that everybody around you believes your explanation.
You may have convinced your family.
But there is One before whom every locked room of the soul stands open.
that should not only terrify you.
For the person who comes to God in repentance, it can also become one of the most comforting truths imaginable.
Because the God who sees the worst thing inside you is the same God from whom you never needed to hide it.
We spend years terrified that if people knew everything about us, they might leave.
We tell testimonies about battles we have already won.
But there are rooms we keep locked.
The resentment toward someone we publicly forgave.
The strange emptiness we feel even while telling everyone how blessed we are.
And sometimes the most exhausting part of sin is not merely committing it.
It is maintaining the person you pretend to be afterward.
Telling everybody “God is good” while quietly wondering how long you can keep living two lives.
He was never fooled by the mask.
And He is not waiting for your confession because He needs information.
He is calling you into confession because you need freedom.
That is why Jeremiah 17 must be read in context.
Before verse 9 ever describes the deceptive heart, verses 5–8 describe two radically different places of trust.
One person trusts in humanity and makes flesh his strength while his heart turns away from the LORD.
בָּרוּךְ הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר יִבְטַח בַּיהוָה וְהָיָה יְהוָה מִבְטַחוֹ
Bārûḵ haggeḇer ʾăšer yiḇṭaḥ baYHWH, wəhāyâ YHWH miḇṭaḥô.
Blessed is the person who trusts in YHWH, whose confidence is YHWH.
Where will you place the weight of your life?
In the impulses of your own heart?
The answer to a deceptive heart is not learning to hate yourself.
The answer is learning where your trust belongs.
“Become suspicious of every emotion you ever experience.”
Bring the heart beneath the authority of the God who searches it.
Let His wisdom overrule your impulses.
Let God tell you when the thing you desperately want is destroying you.
Because sometimes grace sounds like comfort.
Sometimes grace closes the door you were begging God to open.
Sometimes grace allows the consequences to become painful enough that pretending is no longer possible.
Sometimes the mercy of God is that He refuses to let you remain comfortably deceived.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have been explaining it away.
But late at night, when the notifications stop and there is nobody left to impress, you know.
You keep saying, “That is just who I am.”
And maybe the reason this article found you tonight is not so you can send Jeremiah 17:9 to somebody else.
Maybe God is asking you to stop reading it with another person’s face in mind.
Maybe this one is about you.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because Jeremiah does not end with diagnosis.
Only a few verses later comes one of the most beautiful cries in the chapter:
רְפָאֵנִי יְהוָה וְאֵרָפֵא הוֹשִׁיעֵנִי וְאִוָּשֵׁעָה כִּי תְהִלָּתִי אָתָּה
Rəp̄āʾēnî YHWH wəʾērā-p̄ēʾ; hōšîʿēnî wəʾiwwāšēʿâ, kî təhillāṯî ʾāttâ.
“Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for You are my praise.”
Not “teach me to hide it better.”
Not “give me enough religious activity that nobody notices.”
Not “make everybody believe I am okay.”
That cry ultimately finds its deepest Christian answer in Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people should try harder to develop better hearts.
The Gospel is far more devastating than that…
Jesus said that evil proceeds from within, from the human heart. He did not flatter humanity about its condition.
But Christ did something infinitely greater than diagnose us.
And then He went to the cross.
The righteousness we could never manufacture…
And the story did not end inside a sealed tomb.
That means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your life.
Your scandal does not have the final word.
Your addiction does not have the final word.
Your adultery does not have the final word.
Your pornography does not have the final word.
Your pride does not have the final word.
Your failure does not have the final word.
Your secret does not have the final word.
Your shame does not have the final word.
But grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is not permission to keep hugging the thing that crucified your Savior.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
Grace takes the person who finally stops saying, “I’m fine,” and teaches him to pray:
Maybe you need that prayer tonight.
Jesus, my heart has deceived me.
I have wanted things You told me to surrender.
I have defended things Your Word calls sin.
I have blamed people for choices that were mine.
I have tried to look alive spiritually while parts of me were dying.
Teach me to trust You more than I trust myself.
And when my heart tells me something different from Your Word…
give me grace to believe You.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle. But perhaps you do need to stop pretending before God.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer realizes that failure does not have to be final.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Not somebody you want to attack with a Bible verse.
Somebody who has mistaken feelings for truth.
Somebody who thinks their secret has made them unreachable.
Because there may come a night when your own heart begins negotiating with something God has already spoken about, and you will need the reminder again:
Your heart is not your Savior. Jesus is.
Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a purchase of God’s favor. It cannot buy salvation.

Scripture gives us an important safeguard: Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual pressure. Paul teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves cheerful giving.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But if Gospel Warrior is feeding your faith, strengthening believers, reaching struggling Christians and seekers, and putting Christ-centered resources into people's hands, then you can freely choose to become one of the people who helps carry that mission forward.
another prodigal can remember the Father’s house…
another ashamed Christian can discover that repentance still has a door…
another seeker can hear about Jesus…
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with something as ordinary as pressing “share.”
Someone whispers the name of Jesus again after years of running.
And suddenly what looked like a simple Facebook share became part of a story only eternity will fully reveal.
But before you leave, remember the verse we started with.
“The heart is deceitful above all things…”
The God who says the heart is difficult for us to understand immediately declares:
And the prophet who knows the sickness of the human heart eventually cries:
Heal me, LORD, and I will be healed. Save me, and I will be saved.
The cross announces that forgiveness is real for those who come to Christ.
Your heart is not trustworthy enough to become your god.
But it is not too hidden for God to search.
Not too wounded for Him to reach.
Not too sinful for Christ to confront.
Not too far gone to repent.
And not beyond the reach of the Savior who still calls sinners home.
So perhaps tonight the bravest prayer you can pray is not:
“Jesus, search my heart…and teach my heart to follow You.”
Because maybe the most dangerous lie your heart ever told you was not that your sin was harmless.
Maybe it was telling you that after everything you have done, Jesus would never want you back.
He still calls sinners to come.
He still forgives those who repent and believe.
And when Jesus takes the pen, the scandal does not get to write the ending.
